description: Artemis Lunar Future is Nikolai Stoloff, an aspiring astrophysicist, working in collaboration with Claude, an AI coding partner from Anthropic.
summary: At the IM-2 landing target near the Moon's south pole, a 14-day mission arriving on 15 November 2026 is sunlit 97% of the time. Arrive one week late and that falls to 63%, with a five-day stretch of darkness. Shadowline is an interactive 3D map that makes trade-offs like this visible in seconds. It draws real sunlight and shadows on NASA LOLA terrain for any date, using Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons. For any site it shows the Sun and Earth against the terrain horizon, including an eye-level horizon view, and counts down to the next sunset or Earthset. Up to four sites can be compared side by side, a launch-slip table shows the same mission arriving 1, 3 and 7 days late, and one button finds the best arrival dates. These percentages are line-of-sight results from terrain models: the share of time the Sun or Earth is above the terrain. They are not power output or radio-link budgets. It runs in any browser, on a phone or a desktop, with nothing to install.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Live light: for any date and time, shows which ground is sunlit and which is in shadow, on real terrain, in real time.
Site test: click the map, type coordinates, or pick a named south-pole site (for example the IM-2 target on Mons Mouton or the Shackleton ridge). The report shows how far the Sun and Earth sit above or below the terrain horizon at the selected time, a countdown to the next sunset or sunrise and the next Earthset or Earthrise, the share of the window in sunlight, the longest dark stretch, the share with Earth in view, the longest loss of contact, slope, a 360 degree horizon view with the Sun and Earth paths, and a timeline you can click to jump in time.
Compare: up to four sites in one side-by-side table, with the best value in each row marked. Change the date and every site updates.
Mission and launch slip: set a mission length and see the same mission arriving on time and 1, 3 and 7 days late. "Find arrival windows" searches the next 60 days for the best arrival dates.
Horizon view: an eye-level panorama from 2 m above the ground, showing the terrain skyline used in the calculations with the Sun and Earth at true size and position.
Heat maps: share of a chosen window (one lunar day, three months or a year) that each spot is sunlit, has Earth above the horizon, or both together. A fourth layer shows slope.
Find best sites: scans the whole map and pins the three best-scoring, well-separated spots.
Open numbers: each report shows how its 0 to 100 score adds up and exports the full time series as a CSV file.
Works on a phone or a desktop, with nothing to install.

HOW IT WORKS
Terrain is NASA's LOLA south-pole elevation data, 512 km across. Each site report uses the 20 m grid within 10 km of the eight named sites and the 80 m grid within 20 km of any other site. The regional map, live shadows and heat maps use the 240 m grid resampled to 250 m. A switch shows heights at true scale or stretched 3x.
The positions of the Sun and Earth in the Moon's sky are read from NASA JPL Horizons (hourly, Nov 2026 to Dec 2027), so Earth's libration is included. Outside those dates they are computed in the browser from an orbit model and the IAU lunar rotation model.
For every map point, a ray is marched towards the Sun and towards Earth over the curved lunar surface. If terrain rises above the ray, that point is blocked. There is no atmosphere in the model. The Sun is treated as a disk, so partial sunlight is counted.
Heat maps repeat that test across the window on the graphics card. The site test measures the horizon in 720 directions around the chosen point and steps through the window hour by hour.
Score: 45% sunlight share, 35% Earth-in-view share, 20% gentle slope (full marks under 5 degrees, none over 15, halved above 15). The formula is shown in the app.

HOW IT WAS CHECKED
The in-browser backup calculation agrees with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.008 degrees over 396 dates, and with NASA's SPICE toolkit (DE440 ephemeris) to 0.004 degrees across 134 dates.
The GPU heat maps agree with the separate site-by-site calculation to 0.1% on average (1% worst case) over 60 random points.

LIMITS (ALSO STATED IN THE APP)
The map covers the south pole out to about 81.6 degrees south.
Terrain detail is 20 m at best (80 m away from the named sites, 250 m for the regional maps): boulders and small craters are not seen, and results can change over a few hundred metres.
"Earth in view" means the centre of Earth is above the terrain horizon for an antenna 2 m above ground. It is not a radio link budget.
Named site coordinates are approximate. The score is a comparison aid, not a mission rule. Research and education only.

BENEFITS AND GOALS
My goal is for Shadowline to help future NASA missions to the Moon. Teams planning a south-pole landing have to deal with limited sunlight for power and limited contact with Earth, and I want them to have better, easier software for comparing landing sites on real terrain. Today it is a research and education tool. I want to keep developing it until it can support real mission planning with real mission data. It can also help teachers and students see why small changes in place or date matter so much at the lunar south pole.

TOOLS
JavaScript, WebGL2 (three.js), astronomy-engine, and Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio) for the one-time terrain conversion. Code: https://github.com/Klauscreates/shadowline

AI USE AND PRIOR WORK
The code was written with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant, directed and reviewed by me. No data or images are AI-generated. Everything in the repository was made during the hackathon.
dataRefs: LOLA south-pole elevation model LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ (NASA GSFC Planetary Geodesy Data Archive)
NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 ephemeris and lunar orientation), used to check Sun and Earth positions
NASA JPL Horizons (hourly Sun and Earth positions as seen from the Moon, Nov 2026 to Dec 2027)
LOLA south-pole elevation models LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ (80 m) and LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ (20 m), NASA GSFC Planetary Geodesy Data Archive
